Title: Multi-Robot Motions in Milliseconds: Vector-Accelerated Primitives for Sampling-Based Planning
Text:
Multi-Robot Motions in Milliseconds: Vector-Accelerated Primitives for
Sampling-Based Planning
James D. Motes1, Marco Morales1,2, and Nancy M. Amato1
Abstract— In this paper, we extend the recent Vector-
Accelerated Motion Planning (VAMP) framework to multi-
robot motion planning (MRMP). We develop two vector-
accelerated primitives, multi-robot MOTIONVALIDATION (MOT-
VAL) and FINDFIRSTCONFLICT (FFC), which exploit SIMD
parallelism within the multi-robot domain. On pure multi-
robot motion validation tests, this achieves over 1100X speedup
in validation time. Additionally, we modify a representative
set of MRMP algorithms to use these new primitives. The
relative speedup for each algorithm is studied on scenarios
with manipulator, rigid body, and heterogeneous teams with
some instances producing multi-robot solutions in the order of
milliseconds and, in many cases, shows planning time speedups
of over 850X.
I. INTRODUCTION
In this paper, we explore efficient adaptations of the
recent single robot Vector-Accelerated Motion Planning
(VAMP) [1] techniques to the multi-robot domain. VAMP
accelerates sampling-based motion planning (SBMP) by
exploiting single instruction/multiple data (SIMD) forward
kinematics (FK) and collision checking (CC) operations
to validate multiple configurations in parallel on the CPU
and produces speedups of up to 500X on standard plan-
ning algorithms. While much of this speedup comes from
the parallelization (and the simplified sphere-based robot
representation that facilitates it [2]), a significant portion
comes from intelligently exploiting parallel state validation
to increase early termination during motion validation. It is
this key insight that we use to guide our design of vector-
accelerated multi-robot motion planning (MRMP).
In this paper, we develop two MRMP validation primi-
tives: MOTIONVALIDATION (MOTVAL), for boolean valida-
tion, and FINDFIRSTCONFLICT (FFC), for discovering the
earliest conflict. Boolean validity is an extension of single
robot validation with the additional concern of robot-robot
collision at timesteps along synchronized motions in addition
to standard robot-obstacle collisions. A collision of any kind
at any timestep invalidates the motion, and early termination
can occur upon discovery of any collision. Finding the first
conflict is required by many algorithms which plan paths
independently and then look for the earliest robot-robot
collision to refine the paths [3], [4], [5]. As replanning paths
can change the motions after a conflict, it is typically wasted
effort to address conflicts occurring later in paths before

For both primitives, we develop strategies to improve
early termination while exploiting SIMD parallelism for
FK and CC operations. We integrate these primitives into
a set of MRMP methods representative of the different

many cases, produce algorithm speedups exceeding 850X.

II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
In this section, we define the motion planning and multi-
robot motion planning (MRMP) problems and discuss algo-
rithms and vector-acceleration for both.
A. Motion Planning
A robot configuration is defined by its degrees-of-freedom
(DOFs). The configuration space Cspace is the set of all robot
configurations in an environment [6]. Motion planning seeks
a continuous path through the free space Cfree. Representing
Cspace explicitly is intractable in the general case [7], [8].
Sampling-based motion planning (SBMP) instead samples
random configurations and motions between them to search
for a path [9], [10]. Configurations are validated by per-
forming forward kinematics (FK) and collision checking
(CC), and motions are validated by discretizing them into
intermediate configurations which are then validated.
Within SBMP, for both single start/goal query algo-
rithms [10] and multi-query algorithms [9], the motion vali-
dation process has historically been the bottleneck. Methods
like the recursive midpoint bisection checking [11] propose
strategies on where to check which aim to quickly find
a witness collision and improve early termination. Others
choose when to check, often deferring validation until a
motion is known to be required [12]. Finally, some methods
improve how many checks can be done at once [1]. We pull
insights from all three for the multi-robot domain.
B. Vector-Accelerated Motion Planning
Vector-Accelerated Motion Planning (VAMP) [1] intro-
duced fine-grained parallelism to SBMP by exploiting
SIMD operations in primitive functions common to SBMP
algorithms. Much of the SIMD modification focused on FK
and CC where batches of configurations can be processed
in parallel on the CPU, enabling high throughput with low
latency. These SIMD FK and CC operations are enabled
by adopting a sphere-based representation of a robot (which
can be generated with [2]). This sphere-based representation
is then given to a tracing compiler which builds specialized
SIMD kernels for that specific robot’s FK and CC oper-
ations. In addition to enabling the SIMD operations, this
simplified geometric representation contributes to the overall
speedup demonstrated in [1].
Beyond the speedup from processing batches of configu-
rations simultaneously, VAMP proposes intelligent construc-
tion of these batches to increase early termination during mo-
tion validation. Instead of linearly scanning from one end of a
motion to the other in batches of consecutive configurations,
batches are created from configurations spatially distributed
evenly along the motion. The validation of these distributed
batches is referred to as a rake. This is an application
of the insights from prior sequential validation methods
that collisions can be discovered faster by distributing CC
along the motion to the batch processing offered by SIMD
operations. More details are provided in the multi-robot
application of the rake approach in Sec. III-A and Fig. 1.
C. Multi-robot Motion Planning
Multi-robot motion planning (MRMP) seeks to find a
collision-free path through the composite configuration space
Ccomp which is the Cartesian product of the individual
robot Cspaces. Most MRMP papers focus on addressing the
exponential growth of Ccomp with the number of robots.
Here, instead we focus on the cost of validation.
A composite configuration is invalid if any individual
robot configuration is in collision with an obstacle, itself, or
another robot. This cost quickly gets dominated by the robot-
robot CCs which scale quadratically with the number of
robots while robot-obstacle CCs scale linearly. Multi-robot
motion validation is still computed by discretizing individual
motions into intermediate configurations. However, each
discrete intermediate corresponds to one timestep as robot-
robot collisions occur in both space and time.
There are two primary multi-robot validity queries: binary
validity and find the first conflict. The binary validity query
simply returns a boolean true/false validity for the entirety of
the set of synchronized robot motions. This is primarily used
by methods which directly apply single robot SBMP to the
multi-robot domain either by directly searching Ccomp [13],
[14], or treating other robots as dynamic obstacles [15].
These motions can be invalidated by either robot-obstacle
or robot-robot collisions. Some methods consider these si-
multaneously [13], while others first compute decoupled
representations valid in the individual robot Cspaces and
constrain multi-robot motions to compositions of these [14],
decoupling robot-obstacle and robot-robot validation (decid-
ing when to validate).
Methods which query for the first conflict typically com-
pute entire paths valid in the individual robot Cspaces and
then use robot-robot collisions (and the timesteps they occur
at) to guide either search [16], [5] or representation construc-
tion [4], [5]. This validity query assumes individual validity
and only checks for synchronized robot-robot collisions, so
no robot-obstacle CCs are needed. It requires the first conflict
in the set of paths as conflict resolution often de-synchronizes
later portions of the paths, undoing prior resolution effort.
Thus, a single robot-robot witness is insufficient, and all
timesteps prior to a conflict must be validated before a
conflict can be determined to be the earliest. It is from the
difference between these two validity queries that we claim
the need for two distinct multi-robot validity primitives:
MOTVAL and FFC based on their query and use of validity
information, and categorize MRMP algorithms by which of
these they use (Table I).
We find that this category naturally extends the typical
taxonomy of MRMP methods into coupled, decoupled, or
hybrid approaches to either representation construction or
search (Table I). In fact, the validity primitive is central to the
implementation of these other design choices. For example,


all coupled searches must use MOTVAL to validate any
motion segment in Ccomp [13] (even when individual validity
is computed separately in decoupled representations [14]).
Even decoupled searches like prioritized planning still use a
variant of MOTVAL to ensure their individual paths do not
collide with higher priority robot motions [15]. Meanwhile,
hybrid methods which typically start decoupled and then
decide when to couple often use conflict information to guide
these decisions [17], [4], [5]. When the representations stay
decoupled [16], [5], only FFC is needed, but when hybrid
approaches build representations in different compositions
of individual robot Cspaces, MOTVAL is again needed to
validate the motion segments in the representation [17], [4].
The set of methods in Table I provides a representative
for each combination of these design choices with vary-
ing strategies for computing robot-obstacle and robot-robot
validity. In Sec. III-C we describe the application of the
new MOTVAL and FFC (and existing VAMP) primitives to
these methods and evaluate the impact in Sec. IV. Many of
these methods have extensions and improvements, but we
attempted to choose a method representing the root of a
method family and believe the improvements will generalize
across most of their variants.
D. Vector-Accelerated Multi-Robot Motion Planning
At the time of this submission, we are aware of one
workshop paper [18] which has studied the straightforward
application of VAMP to Composite RRT-C and the speedup
of a hybrid search multi-agent pathfinding method adapted
to MRMP [16]. While these naturally use the MOTVAL and
FFC primitives, no such distinction is made in [18], and
only a discussion of vectorized state validity is provided.
Additionally, we consider not only the straightforward appli-
cation of this state validity to sequences of states (in raked
or linear scans) but different strategies for the ordering of
robot-obstacle vs robot-robot CC across the motion.
In this manuscript, in addition to providing distinct vector-
accelerated primitive functions for the two classes, we study
the impact of those functions across a set of MRMP al-
gorithms representative of the different ways robot-obstacle
and robot-robot CCs are performed. Additionally, while the
workshop paper [18] studies the impact of vector-accelerated
state validity for multi-robot systems on several manipulator
domains (including impressive results on multi-arm assem-
bly), we study the difference in impact on planning times
for manipulators, rigid body, and heterogeneous teams with
increasing numbers of robots. We are not aware of any peer-
reviewed publication studying the adaptation of VAMP [1]
to the multi-robot domain.
III. METHODOLOGY
In this section, we provide two vector-accelerated MRMP
primitives: MOTVAL (Sec. III-A) and FFC (Sec. III-B). We
then describe how a representative set of MRMP algorithms
can utilize these modified primitives (Sec. III-C).
A. Motion Validation
The multi-robot MOTVAL primitive (Alg. 1) is used when
the algorithm cares only for the boolean validity of a set
of robot paths P. As described in Section II-C, this is
usually in coupled approaches where the movement of all
robots is being considered at once. A variant of it is also
used in decoupled, prioritized planning when the validity
of motion segments for a single robot need to be checked
against the already planned motions of higher priority robots
(discussed in Section III-C.2). In either case, the objective
is to discover a witness collision as early as possible if one
exists, optimizing early termination. This can be achieved by
either a robot-obstacle collision or a robot-robot collision.
During empirical evaluation, we have seen the likelihood
of which collision type can be discovered faster vary with
the number of robots and the density of obstacles, so we
present two different strategies: combined and hierarchical.
The combined approach checks robot-obstacle and robot-
robot validity for each batch of timesteps before moving
onto the next batch of timesteps (this is a straightforward
application of the state-based validation discussed in [18]).
Hierarchical first performs all robot-obstacle validation and
then all robot-robot validation. Intuitively, robot-obstacle
collisions are more likely when there are more obstacles or
more robots to collide with those obstacles. Note that robot-
obstacle validation also checks the robot for self-collision.
We provide a study of the different strategies in Sec. IV-B.1.
Alg. 1 uses a set of underlying VAMP functions. PACK-
CFGBATCH takes in a path pi, a batch index b, and a
packing strategy (either rake or linear). The rake strategy
temporally distributes timesteps evenly along the path (as is
done with the spatial distribution in VAMP [1]). For batch

B. Find First Conflict
The FFC primitive is used when collision information
is required to guide either representation construction or
search (typically a hybrid method of some kind). This
requires discovering the first timestep at which any robot-
robot collision occurs in the set of paths P (rather than any
collision witness).
In addition to the return type, there are two main distinc-
tions between MOTVAL in Alg. 1 and FFC in Alg. 2. First,
FFC does not consider robot-obstacle collisions. It assumes
that all paths are free of robot-obstacle collisions and is only
searching for robot-robot collisions (all SPHERESFK calls
return spheres in the world frame).
Second, it uses the linear strategy for packing configura-
tion batches (lines 7, 10). As a conflict at timestep tconflict
can only be confirmed as the first conflict if all timesteps
t < tconflict are collision-free, validation must be performed
for timesteps 0, ..., tconflict. Thus, employing the rake strategy
which temporally distributes timestep batches evenly along
the paths will result in validation effort spent on timesteps
t > tconflict (with the exception of tconflict = tmax). Taking
a linear packing approach ensures the minimum number
of timestep batches are validated before discovering tconflict.
For simplicity of notation, we leave the extraction of the
individual timestep tconflict within the batch of consecutive
configurations in the CC function call.
C. Application in MRMP Algorithms
Here we provide a brief description of how the represen-
tative set of algorithms in Table I use our new multi-robot
primitives or primitives from single robot VAMP [1]. The
“Validity Query” row in Table I provides a quick summary
for which algorithms use either MOTVAL or FFC.
1) Composite RRT-C: Composite RRT-C is a direct ap-
plication of the single robot RRT-C [19] in Ccomp. The
implementation mirrors the RRT-C implementation in [1]


with the multi-robot MOTVAL primitive replacing the single
robot version.
2) PP-ST-RRT: Prioritized planning [20] with Space Time
RRT [21] plans for robots sequentially in a fixed priority or-
der (referred to as PP-ST-RRT) [15]. Higher priority paths are
treated as dynamic obstacles for lower priority paths using
ST-RRT. The MOTVAL primitive in ST-RRT is replaced with
a modified version of Alg. 1. As PP-ST-RRT plans for one
robot at a time, the outer loop on line 17 is replaced with only
the current robot and the inner loop on line 20 iterates over
only higher priority robots. We simplify the implementation
of ST-RRT here and do not include the rewiring mechanisms
as many of the other algorithms seek only to find a valid path,
though we expect the relative performance gains to hold.
3) ST-CBS: ST-CBS [5] modifies the ST-RRT [21] logic
to work within the Conflict-Based Search (CBS) frame-
work [3]. CBS builds a constraint tree (CT) where nodes
contain sets of constraints for each robot and paths which ad-
here to those constraints. The search evaluates the paths in a
node for conflicts, and, if none are discovered, returns a valid
solution. Upon discovering a conflict between robots ri, rj,
a constraint is generated for each, and the CT branches,
creating two new nodes, one with an additional constraint
for ri and one with an additional constraint for rj.
ST-CBS utilizes a unidirectional ST-RRT (UST-RRT)
method to generate the individual paths. We point the reader
to the manuscript for the algorithmic details [5], but the
basic primitives function the same as those in ST-RRT
with constraints forming obstacles in space-time which can
be represented as instantaneous (or short-lived) dynamic
obstacles. Additionally, the new FFC primitive is employed
to search for conflicts between paths when evaluating nodes
in the CT.
4) MR-dRRT:

IV. EVALUATION
We conduct a set of experiments to evaluate the impact
of the vector-acclerated multi-robot primitives on both pure
validation and MRMP algorithm performance. Section IV-A
describes our experimental design and Section IV-B reports
the results of each experiment.

A. Experimental Design
The experiments are designed to evaluate the three claims
made in this paper: (i) vector-accelerated multi-robot prim-
itives improve validation time, (ii) they improve MRMP
algorithm runtimes, and (iii) MOTVAL and FFC should be
distinct primitives.
For (i) and (iii), we include a validation timing experiment
in Section IV-B.1 which isolates the runtime of validating
a set of randomly generated motions for a group of panda
manipulators in an environment depicted in Fig. 2. The per-
formance of the different MOTVAL strategies and baselines
using the Flexible Collision Library (FCL) [22] and sphere-
based validation are compared to characterize the impact of
each design choice.
For (ii), we include planning problems with manipulator,
rigid body, and heterogeneous teams (Sec. IV-B.2, IV-B.3,
and IV-B.4). For each of these, we report the runtimes
of the representative set of algorithms listed in Table I,
each with the new primitives enabled and the baseline FCL
and sphere-based CC implementations. The different team
compositions demonstrate the difference in impact based on
robot complexity and coordination requirements.
Results for these scenarios are reported in Fig. 5. Addi-
tionally, the relative speedup for each algorithm is reported in
Fig. 4 and 6. These report the average speedup across trials
for which an algorithm was successful with both collision
backends (VAMP vs FCL, VAMP vs Sphere). This is
to avoid penalizing faster configurations for solving harder
problems (which can be obscured in the plots).
The new vector-accelerated primitives, the baseline FCL
and sphere-based CC implementations, and the MRMP
algorithm implementations are written in C++ and build on
the recently released OMPL 2.0 [23] with native VAMP
integrations. The implementations will be made open-source
upon acceptance of this paper to maintain a double-blind
review. All experiments were conducted on a single Linux
workstation (x86 64, kernel 6.8) equipped with an Intel Core
i7-14700F CPU (up to 5.4 GHz) and 32 GB of RAM.

the CAGE environment depicted in Fig. 2. We also consider
the same manipulator arrangements without obstacles to
isolate the computation of robot-robot collision checking.
We evaluate the performance of both hierarchical and com-
bined robot-obstacle and robot-robot validation strategies.
Additionally, we test both approaches with rake and linear
packing strategies to measure the impact of the different
design decisions. We report the percentage of validation
effort performed by each variant as the number of CC calls
made before early termination out of all possible CCs for
the motions. The same motions are validated with baseline
FCL and sphere-based CC implementations with sequential
linear scans to measure the relative performance (Fig. 3).
The two most impressive results come from the 1109X
speedup over FCL by the combined rake approach for
4 robots with obstacles and the 0.2% evaluation before
termination achieved by the hierarchical rake for either 16
robot variation. Overall, we see significant performance gains
compared to FCL. All strategies show a speedup from the
sphere-based approach, and either implementation of the rake
packing strategy outperformed the linear approach, demon-
strating the impact of both SIMD batching and the rake
packing strategy for multi-robot validation. Additionally,
the linear packing approach is equivalent to adding robot-
obstacle validation to the FFC primitive, demonstrating the
benefit of maintaining a distinct MOTVAL primitive with
strategies like raking.
The presence of obstacles has a greater impact on the hier-
archical strategy, as expected, with the evaluated percentage
being notably lower in the tests with obstacles, as individ-
ual validation is still conducted to check for self-collision.
Though, as the number of robots increases, the probability
of at least one self-collision occurring increases to the point
where individual validation again leads to early termination.
While both the hierarchical and combined strategies can ter-
minate early from individual robot collisions, the hierarchical
strategy rakes through the linearly increasing robot-obstacle
CCs first, while the combined strategy incurs the cost of
the quadratically increasing robot-robot CCs to reach the
same individual collision. The benefit of this behavior is
reversed when early batches contain robot-robot collisions
as hierarchical performs all robot-obstacle validation before
checking for any robot-robot collision.
Additionally, Fig. 3 shows improving early termination as
the number of robots increase. While not included in the
table, the hierarchical rake validation of the 16 manipulator
scenarios reported the smallest total validation time despite
the highest number of robots. We use the hierarchical rake
MOTVAL strategy for the rest of the evaluation.
2) Manipulator Coordination: Two rows of Panda manip-
ulators have randomly sampled start and goal poses with their
end-effectors inside the cage (Fig. 2). Conflicts often emerge
between manipulators adjacent or across from each other.
Five random start and goal sets (or tasks) are generated,
and each algorithm configuration is run with the same ten
seeds on each task for a total of 50 trials each. Each trial
is given 1000s. Variance between configurations of the same
algorithm is limited to validation effort.
Figs. 5a and 5b shows the performance of each algorithm
planning for 4 and 8 Panda manipulators. As expected, there
is a significant improvement in planning time and success
rate across all algorithms. Composite RRT-C and ST-CBS
demonstrate the greatest improvement with a speedup of
over 850X (Fig. 4a). The other methods also experience
significant speedups for the 4 manipulator scenario (338X,
453X, and 178X for PP-ST-RRT, MR-dRRT, and ARC
respectively). As ARC (with vector-accelerated primitives)
was the only method to solve a significant percentage of the
8 manipulator tasks, we tested it with 16 robots (as depicted
in Fig. 2) over five tasks run with three seeds each. It solved
5/6 trials on two of the tasks (and none for the others) with
a median solve time of 9.4s. The small solve times on the
successful trials and failure to solve the other tasks within
the 1000s indicates the difficulty lies in the search for these
large problems rather than the validation cost.
3) Rigid Body Coordination: Two lines of flying sphere
robots must swap places with each other. This arrangement
naturally induces N

flicts emerge as a result of conflict resolution and avoidance.

random seeds. Each trial is given 100s.

problems with 4, 8, 16, and 32 robots. Here we see a smaller
impact using the primitives compared to the manipulator

Interestingly, we see the relative speedup increase as the
number of robots increase for all algorithms except PP-ST-
RRT. In addition to the exponential growth Composite RRT-

the number of robots increases, the number of robot-robot

also applies to the effort to find conflicts in ST-CBS and

As ARC again demonstrated the fastest planning times

evaluate the same scenario with 64 and 128 robots (still with

4) Heterogeneous Coordination: Two groups of flying
sphere robots must pass through a corridor of Panda ma-
nipulators as described in Fig. 2b. We ran 10 trials with
each method configuration with a 1000s time limit. The
planning times, success rates, and algorithm speedups are
reported in Figs. 5g, 5h, and 6. The methods which attempt
higher levels of coordination struggle here with PP-ST-RRT
significantly outperforming the other methods. The priority
order here is a significant design choice. We planned first for
the manipulators and then for the flying spheres. Reversing
this priority order results in PP-ST-RRT failing to find any
solutions within the time limit. The significance of the
speedup provided by the primitive is evident here with the
130-150X speedup for PP-ST-RRT resulting in plans in less
than a second for the 4 Panda–8 flying sphere scenario.
As with ARC in the prior two scenarios, we push PP-ST-
RRT on larger teams, testing it with 16 Panda manipulators
and 32 flying spheres. It was able to solve 6/30 trials with a
median runtime of 16.3s with vector-accelerated primitives
and 67.2s with the sphere-based representation.
V. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we have demonstrated that how you apply
vector-acceleration to multi-robot validation matters, devel-
oped several strategies for doing so, and evaluated the relative
speedup they offers across a representative set of algorithms
on varied problem settings. We see two avenues for future
work: (i) further investigation of when, where, and how many
to validate including how to leverage further parallelization
with the GPU as has been done in the single robot domain,
and (ii) take advantage of decreased validation costs to use
validity as a signal, expanding on the conflict-driven planning
of approaches like ARC [4]. Open-source code of the vector-
accelerated primitives and MRMP algorithms will be made
available upon paper acceptance.

Abstract: In this paper, we extend the recent Vector- Accelerated Motion Planning (VAMP) framework to multi- robot motion planning (MRMP). We develop two vector- accelerated primitives, multi-robot MOTIONVALIDATION (MOT- VAL) and FINDFIRSTCONFLICT (FFC), which exploit SIMD parallelism within the multi-robot domain. On pure multi- robot motion validation tests, this achieves over 1100X speedup in validation time. Additionally, we modify a representative set of MRMP algorithms to use these new primitives. The relative speedup for each algorithm is studied on scenarios with manipulator, rigid body, and heterogeneous teams with some instances producing multi-robot solutions in the order of milliseconds and, in many cases, shows planning time speedups of over 850X.
